claims.text: Higher lattice distortion in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles impedes atomic diffusion.
Higher lattice distortion impedes phase segregation in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Lattice distortion governs nanoparticle structural and chemical stability at high operating temperatures.
The proposed starting materials are near-equiatomic, multi-element, single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles.
Changing composition changes atomic-size mismatch and thereby modulates lattice distortion.
The specified 773–1173 K and 473–1923 K thermal regimes are relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric service, respectively.
Atomic-size mismatch produces local strain fields that manifest as lattice distortion.
Increased lattice distortion creates heterogeneous strain fields.
Heterogeneous strain fields slow dislocation motion.
Heterogeneous strain fields slow atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion retards phase and elemental segregation during high-temperature service.
Retarded segregation preserves the single-phase structure and chemical homogeneity.
Higher-distortion nanoparticles will undergo less phase change and smaller compositional fluctuations than lower-distortion nanoparticles after equivalent thermal aging.
Higher-distortion nanoparticles will retain greater structural integrity after thermal aging.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch will exhibit more phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed relationship is limited to near-equiatomic, initially single-phase nanoparticles under inert or otherwise controlled atmospheres with minimal oxidation and poisoning.
Particle size and synthesis-induced defects may modify the effect of lattice distortion on stability.
The cited evidence concerns a near-equiatomic bulk Nb-Ta-Ti-V refractory high-entropy alloy that remains a single BCC solid solution through testing at 900 °C.
Analogous bulk high-entropy-alloy studies support a causal role for lattice distortion in high-temperature stability.
Comparable segregation or degradation in the high- and low-distortion sets would falsify the claim that increased lattice distortion governs stability.
